PointMIL:

Interpretable Point‑Cloud Classification using Multiple Instance Learning

Three‑dimensional point clouds are ubiquitous in science and industry, yet many state‑of‑the‑art classifiers behave as opaque black boxes. PointMIL introduces an inherently interpretable framework that leverages multiple instance learning (MIL) to jointly improve accuracy and provide fine‑grained, point‑level explanations.

Overview Method Datasets Results Conclusion BibTeX

Overview

Conventional point‑cloud classification models achieve impressive performance but often lack transparency. Our framework, PointMIL, is designed from the ground up to be interpretable: each point in a cloud receives an importance weight learned through multiple instance learning. These weights are used both to aggregate point features into a global representation and to visualise the regions that drive each prediction.

We evaluate PointMIL on several public benchmarks and a new biomedical dataset, showing that our method not only surpasses baselines in accuracy but also yields meaningful point‑wise explanations. On the IntrA dataset, PointMIL attains a mean class accuracy of 97.3 % and an F1 score of 97.5 %, outperforming standard backbones by a large margin.

Method

The core of PointMIL is a novel MIL pooling strategy. Each point is assigned an importance score via a lightweight scoring network. These scores scale or re‑weight point features before aggregation, producing a bag‑level representation that highlights the most informative points. The same scores serve as interpretable saliency maps, enabling point‑level inspection of predictions.

We explore several pooling variants. Additive and Conjunctive pooling scale point features by their importance weights; Instance and Attention schemes rely on attention mechanisms and provide weaker class‑specific explanations. Across backbones, additive and conjunctive pooling deliver the best trade‑off between accuracy and interpretability.

Datasets

We benchmark our approach on four public datasets and introduce a new biomedical collection:

  • IntrA: annotated vascular models used for interpretability and classification.
  • Red Blood Cells (RBC): nine classes of red blood cells grouped by morphology.
  • ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN: standard benchmarks of everyday objects used to demonstrate generalisation.
  • Morph3DCell: a dataset of 1 500 drug‑treated cancer cells captured with oblique‑plane light‑sheet microscopy. Cells were treated with Nocodazole, Blebbistatin or left untreated, enabling us to study how treatments alter 3D cell morphology.

Results

Across datasets and backbones, PointMIL consistently improves both interpretability and accuracy. On IntrA, our method achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance with mACC = 97.3 % and F1 = 97.5 %. On the RBC dataset we observe up to an 11.3 % improvement in mean class accuracy over baselines.

On the Morph3DCell dataset, PointMIL not only classifies treatments but also reveals biologically meaningful shape differences. Interpretations for Blebbistatin‑treated cells highlight elongated protrusions consistent with myosin II inhibition, whereas Nocodazole‑treated cells emphasise the cell periphery, reflecting microtubule depolymerisation.

The table below summarises the classification results on IntrA for selected backbones with and without PointMIL. The improvements (shown in parentheses) demonstrate that our pooling enhances each backbone.

Backbone mACC (baseline) mACC (PointMIL) F1 (baseline) F1 (PointMIL)
PointNet 79.1 82.2 (+3.1) 78.8 81.1 (+2.3)
DGCNN 80.5 85.1 (+4.6) 80.2 84.2 (+4.0)
CurveNet† 83.6 83.1 (‑0.5) 83.1 82.9 (‑0.2)
PointMLP 80.1 87.1 (+7.0) 79.4 86.4 (+7.0)

Conclusion

PointMIL unifies interpretability and performance for point‑cloud classification. By integrating multiple instance learning into existing backbones, it achieves high accuracy while providing local explanations for each point. Our experiments on biomedical and synthetic datasets demonstrate that interpretability and performance need not be traded off. Future work includes extending the framework to segmentation tasks, incorporating uncertainty estimates and applying it to high‑content screening and robotics.
